A.explanation: This corresponds to a distance of $1.5\lambda$, which miscounts the integer number of $\lambda$ spacings between successive wavefronts from GH to P.

B.explanation: This corresponds to a distance of $2\lambda$, which counts only two spacings and stops one wavefront short of the curved wavefront through P.

C.explanation: GH is three $\lambda$ spacings from the wavefront through P, so distance $3\lambda$ at speed $c$ takes time $3\lambda/c$.

D.explanation: This corresponds to a distance of $4\lambda$, which adds one extra spacing beyond the wavefront through P.

hints: Notice the four drawn wavefronts: plane wavefront GH, the plane wavefront at the barrier, the small diffracted wavefront, and the large diffracted wavefront through P.
Recall successive wavefronts of a monochromatic wave are one wavelength $\lambda$ apart along the direction of travel.
Count how many $\lambda$ steps GH must travel to reach P, then use $time = distance/c$ with distance as a multiple of $\lambda$.
walkthrough: Identify GH as the starting plane wavefront on the left and P as a point on the outermost diffracted circular wavefront on the right.
State the rule that successive wavefronts represent positions of the same phase one period apart, so their spatial separation is one wavelength $\lambda$.
Count the spacings: GH to the plane front at the barrier is $\lambda$, to the small diffracted front is $2\lambda$, to the large front through P is $3\lambda$.
The shortest distance some portion of GH must travel to reach P is therefore $s = 3\lambda$, with diffraction spreading energy sideways to P but the radial distance still counted in $\lambda$ steps.
Use $s = c t$, so $t = s/c = 3\lambda/c$ with units of $\text{m}/\text{m s}^{-1} = \text{s}$.
